claims.claim: Planar two-exit instances admit a cyclic two-gate decomposition. Let the exits be p,q and let B=N(p)∩N(q). Every component of G−({p,q}∪B) is adjacent to at most two vertices of B; when |B|≥3, those two are consecutive in the cyclic order of B around the exits.
claims.evidence: Fix a plane embedding and retain the K_{2,|B|} subgraph H on {p,q}∪B. For k=|B|≥3, H is 2-connected, with v=k+2, e=2k, and hence f=k. Its facial boundaries are cycles; simplicity and bipartiteness give length at least four, while their total length is 2e=4k. Thus every face is a 4-cycle p-b_i-q-b_j-p. Its two B-vertices are consecutive in the rotations at both exits. The drawing of any connected component disjoint from H lies in one face of H, and each attachment edge remains in that face's closure, so the component can meet only those two gates. For k≤2 the bound is immediate.
claims.search_method: Direct plane-embedding, Euler-formula, and facial-boundary proof, including the small-|B| cases.

claims.claim: There is a linear-time classification when the exits have the same independent neighborhood. After deleting a possible irrelevant edge pq, suppose N(p)=N(q)=B and B is independent. The fugitive wins exactly when (i) s∈{p,q}∪B, (ii) s has a neighbor in B, or (iii) s has a neighbor w having two distinct neighbors in B.
claims.evidence: Conditions (i) and (ii) give an immediate exit or a move to a gate with two intact exit edges. Under (iii), after moving to w, the two triples {wb_i,b_ip,b_iq} are edge-disjoint, so one entire triple survives Nemesis's first deletion; moving through that gate then survives the next deletion. Conversely, when none holds, the first reached outside vertex sees at most one gate. Its original outside component has at most two boundary gates by claim 0. Nemesis initially deletes one exit edge at a visible gate, or at an arbitrary boundary gate if none is visible. Thereafter at most one fresh boundary gate can become newly reachable after an outside-to-outside move, so that deletion prepares it; entering a prepared gate lets Nemesis delete its other exit edge. From a dead gate, B-independence forces the next move into one outside component, whose only possible other boundary gate can immediately be prepared. This invariant prevents entry into any gate with two intact exit edges. Exact edge deletion guarantees finite termination, and a component with no boundary gate is already losing. Marking B, counting B-neighbors, and scanning s and N(s) takes linear time.
claims.search_method: Direct strategy/invariant proof plus exhaustive exact Boolean minimax testing on every listed labeled two-gate graph with up to four gates and three outside vertices.

claims.claim: Two broader target-relevant subclasses are linearly solvable: (a) the graph induced by regular vertices is a forest, with arbitrary degrees; or (b) every regular vertex has degree at most three, with arbitrary exit degrees.
claims.evidence: A start at an exit is immediately winning, and exit-exit edges cannot help the fugitive and need never be chosen by an optimal Nemesis. For every regular-to-exit incidence vx, replace vx by an edge from v to a distinct exit leaf and remove the original exits. Before termination the fugitive occupies only regular vertices; regular moves, terminal exit moves, and relevant Nemesis deletions therefore correspond edge-for-edge. Connectivity to some original exit is equivalent to connectivity through the regular core to some new leaf. In case (a), adjoining leaves to a regular forest leaves a forest, so the start component is a tree. In case (b), every regular degree is preserved and every new exit has degree one, so the transformed graph has maximum degree at most three. The source's linear-time algorithms for trees and simple maximum-degree-three graphs apply, and the transformation is linear-size.
claims.search_method: Direct outcome-preserving reduction proof and exhaustive exact comparison over all 1,024 simple graphs on three regular vertices and two exits, including an optional exit-exit edge.

claims.claim: The binary-escape-tree condition is not necessary even for planar simple graphs with exactly two exits. A seven-vertex counterexample has exits p,q, start s, regular vertices a,b,c,z, and edges pa,pb,qa,qb,ab,az,bz,bc,cz,cs.
claims.evidence: Exact integer orientation tests validate the stated crossing-free drawing. The fugitive moves s→c. If the first deletion is bc, he moves c→z; one further deletion cannot damage both edge-disjoint triples {za,ap,aq} and {zb,bp,bq}, so an intact triple yields escape. Otherwise bc survives and he moves c→b. If bp or bq remains after the second deletion, he exits; if both are gone, they are exactly the first two deletions, so b→a leaves both ap and aq intact before the next single deletion. After exit duplication, the only possible roots within distance one of s are s and c. Vertex s has graph degree one. A tree rooted at c cannot use regular leaf s, so its children must be b,z. Then nonroot z, whose neighbors are a,b,c, would require both a and the already-used sibling b as children, creating a cycle rather than a tree. Hence the tree condition fails.
claims.witness: Vertices p,q,s,a,b,c,z; edges pa,pb,qa,qb,ab,az,bz,bc,cz,cs; integer coordinates a=(0,0), b=(120,0), p=(60,80), q=(60,-80), z=(60,40), c=(90,10), s=(80,23); winning first move s→c.
claims.search_method: Exact segment-incidence testing, exhaustive minimax evaluation against all deletions, validation of the stated second-move policy, and exhaustive enumeration of 2,048 split-graph edge-subset/root candidates.

claims.claim: An exact recurrence gives PSPACE membership and an O*(8^n) planar algorithm, although not a polynomial classification. For deleted-edge set D and current regular vertex v, W(D,v) holds iff some surviving move vw reaches an exit or, for every surviving edge e Nemesis might delete, w remains connected to an exit and W(D∪{e},w) holds.
claims.evidence: Backward induction on the number of surviving edges proves the recurrence: the fugitive existentially selects vw; reaching an exit wins before deletion, while a regular w is winning exactly if every legal Nemesis deletion preserves exit-connectivity and leaves a winning continuation. Each recursive call increases |D|, so the recursion is acyclic. There are at most n·2^m states and polynomial work per transition. Memoization therefore gives O*(2^m) time. Depth-first evaluation has depth at most m and polynomial-size state and iterator frames, establishing PSPACE membership without storing the full table. For a simple planar graph with n≥3, m≤3n−6, hence O*(2^m)=O*(8^n); smaller graphs are constant-size.
claims.search_method: Formal backward-induction proof plus exhaustive comparison with a separately phased Fugitive/Nemesis evaluator on all graph, deleted-edge-set, and position states for five labeled vertices.

target_evidence: The exact target requires either a polynomial-time classification for all planar simple graphs with exactly two exits or a matching hardness result. The draft explicitly says that it obtained neither. Claims 0–2 give genuine structural leverage and linear algorithms only for restricted subclasses; claim 3 supplies a relevant obstruction to one proposed certificate; and claim 4 gives only a general exponential algorithm and PSPACE upper bound. These are material, correct advances but do not settle the requested classification. Because the final writeup labels itself partial, identifies the unresolved general core, and does not headline a full target solution, its claimed_resolution of PARTIAL is accurate rather than overstated or understated.
checks_performed: Read only the authorized source input and iteration-2 draft; used no web, retrieval database, receipt, prior run, verification report, or other solution.
